selected.name: Self-contained announcement quality
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the text is a coherent, dated announcement with an identifiable subject, issuing organization, news peg, and complete supporting details; score 0 when it is merely a product page, listicle, fragment, or generic informational page.
selected.rationale: R04, R22, and R43 explicitly lack identifiable press-release bodies, whereas R35 is a compact, clearly dated corporate announcement.

selected.name: Serious dramatic incident with significant stakes
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the release recounts a specific, time-and-place-bound dramatic incident involving physical danger, legal jeopardy, large-scale harm, or criminal conduct. Score 0 if no specific incident is described or if the incident is minor and inconsequential.
selected.rationale: R49 (a Gigafactory trespasser running over a Tesla employee, resulting in felony arrests) and R09/R53 (a payment-card breach affecting tens of millions of customers) score dense_high. R54 (180 passengers walked through an airport without passport checks but no harm resulted) scores dense_low despite having an 'incident' frame—the dense model appears to weigh whether the stakes are genuinely significant.
member_names: Serious dramatic incident with significant stakes
Specified, unresolved conflict with a named external institution

selected.name: Breadth of public or consumer impact
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the announced change directly and tangibly affects a large population of ordinary consumers or workers (millions of shoppers, all employees company-wide, entire user base). Score 0 if the audience affected is narrow (a single executive, a small community of enthusiasts, an internal team).
selected.rationale: R03 (Target Deal Days sale reaching millions of shoppers), R52 (Airbnb's live/work-anywhere policy for all employees and guests), and R58 (debt-free degrees for 340,000 Target team members) score dense_high. R17 (a single C-suite appointment) and R35 (one on-site childcare center) score dense_low, suggesting the scorecard may credit formal significance while the dense model weighs how many real people are affected.
member_names: Breadth of public or consumer impact
Scale of population or market directly affected

selected.name: Cross-industry or ecosystem-wide implications
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the announcement has direct consequences for multiple companies, entire industries, supply chains, or regulatory regimes—not just the issuing organization. Score 0 if the implications are confined entirely to the issuer's internal operations with no spillover effects.
selected.rationale: R56 (opening the charging standard to all automakers and networks) reshapes an entire industry's infrastructure. R01 (all Teslas get self-driving hardware) affects autonomous driving broadly. R05 (battery recycling supply gap) touches EV makers, miners, and recyclers globally. Low-dense items like R37 (IdeaExchange redesign) and R60 (one childcare center) affect essentially nobody outside the company.
member_names: Changes options for competitors, regulators or an entire market

selected.name: Cultural crossover or named celebrity figure
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the release features a recognizable celebrity, public figure, or cultural institution (entertainer, major media programme, public official) that extends the story well beyond the usual corporate beat. Score 0 if all named individuals are company executives, analysts, or unknown private parties.
selected.rationale: R46 (Seth Rogen hosting an Airbnb stay) and R13 (Tesla suing the BBC's Top Gear) score dense_high—both carry crossover appeal that would interest entertainment and culture desks, not just industry reporters. Almost all dense_low items (R08, R28, R35, R43) name only internal executives, limiting their reach.
member_names: Cultural crossover or named celebrity figure
Recognizable public figure or celebrity involvement

selected.name: Distinctive human-interest access
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the release offers unusual access to a recognizable person, remarkable place, or scarce experience with vivid concrete particulars; score 0 when it presents a routine product or corporate activity.
selected.rationale: R51 combines Seth Rogen, a creative studio, and limited overnight stays; R01 uses unusual homes and visual settings, while R52 turns a product concept into an attention-grabbing joke.

selected.name: Operational commitment at scale
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the text specifies substantial resources, coverage, staffing, rollout, or enforcement that make an initiative materially real; score 0 when it is primarily an aspiration, intention, or symbolic statement.
selected.rationale: R15 specifies standards, enforcement channels, investment, and implementation timing; R32 specifies $200 million, 340,000 workers, and hundreds of programs; R35 details a multiyear store rollout.

selected.name: Distinctive quotable voice rather than interchangeable corporate template
selected.instruction: Score the register of the writing itself. 10 = an unmistakable authorial voice a reporter would quote verbatim for its manner -- sustained satire, an abrupt one-word sign-off, unhedged internal candour, jokes that land -- copy that no other organisation's communications function could have produced. 5 = competent house style with a few lines that stand out. 0 = fully templated: dateline, ticker, benefit-laden subheads, 'About [Company]' block, and not one sentence anyone would reproduce for how it is written. Judge only manner of expression; a release with no facts at all can still score 10 here, and a fact-rich release can score 0.
selected.rationale: R01 (dense 0.686 / card 0.348) is a wholly satirical product announcement containing essentially no verifiable fact -- every substance-shaped criterion must mark it down, while a reader recognises copy that writes itself up. R25 and R39 (0.906 / ~0.34) carry lines like 'that is insanely badass' inside an otherwise routine personnel announcement, and R06 (0.857 / 0.123) closes a standards release with the single word 'Enjoy.' The scorecard has no way to register voice as evidence of anything, so it reads all three as thin.
member_names: Distinctive human voice, humor, or dramatic flair
Distinctive quotable voice rather than interchangeable corporate template

selected.name: Concrete actionability for consumers or users
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the release tells the audience something they can immediately act on—buy a product today, make a reservation, apply for a benefit, use a new feature, access a service—with specific dates, prices, or URLs. Score 0 if the release describes something abstract, internal, or future with no way for the reader to act.
selected.rationale: R01 (customers can buy today), R46 (Model 3 reservations opening March 31 with exact time and link), R38 (Target Deal Days with exact dates and shopping methods), R57 (book Seth Rogen stay at specific URL and price). These create immediate reader action. Contrast R37 (internal IdeaExchange redesign) or R55 (office reopening principles) where the reader can do nothing.
member_names: Concrete actionability for consumers or users

selected.name: First disclosure here, not restatement of already-public facts
selected.instruction: Score whether the central fact appears to be entering the public record with this document. 10 = the core claim is disclosed here, with no indication the audience already knows it and no dependence on a prior announcement to make sense. 5 = a genuinely new increment attached to a substantial recap of prior announcements. 0 = the text openly concedes the news is old -- 'as you have likely heard by now', 'in August 2020 we announced a temporary ban ... today we are officially codifying it', 'last month our CEO announced X ... today we're announcing three steps forward' -- or the body is essentially a chronology of initiatives launched in previous years. Judge only novelty of disclosure within the text, not importance.
selected.rationale: R12 (dense 0.478 / card 0.887) is explicit that the ban it announces has been in force since August 2020 and is merely being 'codified'. R13, R41 and R58 (dense 0.317, 0.299, 0.299 against card 0.737, 0.773, 0.773) all open by telling the reader 'as you have likely heard by now'. R28 (0.515 / 0.915) frames itself as follow-through on last month's announcement. Completeness- and context-shaped criteria positively reward this recap structure, because a restatement is by construction well-supported and well-contextualised.
member_names: First disclosure here, not restatement of already-public facts

selected.name: Formal filing or legally consequential step by the issuer
selected.instruction: Score whether the item is, or reports, an act by the issuer that has legal force. 10 = a registration statement submitted to a securities regulator under a cited rule, an action filed in court, meeting machinery that carries legal effect (record dates, control numbers, legal proxies, a stated password and deadline), a specification lodged with standards bodies. 5 = a policy that binds the issuer's users with stated enforcement consequences and effective dates. 0 = communication with no legal standing at all: a blog post, a marketing announcement, an aspiration with no instrument behind it. Judge legal consequence, not the readability of the legal language.
selected.rationale: R55 (dense 0.799 / card 0.352) is nothing but a Rule 135 notice and disclaimer, and the scorecard reads it as thin boilerplate; R51 (0.792 / 0.311) is pure procedural machinery -- control numbers, legal proxies, a submission deadline; R43 (0.761 / 0.399) opens on a filed libel action. Criteria for prose quality, engagement and accessibility treat statutory language as bad writing, which exactly inverts its significance: the more constrained the language, the more binding the act it records.
member_names: Formal filing or legally consequential step by the issuer

selected.name: Direct incident facts vs. reassurance-letter voice
selected.instruction: Score whether a release describing a harm or crisis affecting third parties (customers, the public) states the hard facts of what happened -- scope, timeline, cause -- plainly and early, versus leading with apology, reassurance, and trust-affirming language that delays or dilutes those facts. A 10 = the incident's who/what/when/scope is stated plainly in the opening sentences, with reassurance language subordinate to it. A 0 = the release opens with and is dominated by apology/reassurance/trust language, with hard facts delayed, minimized, or given only in passing.
selected.rationale: R02, R35, and R38 are the identical Target 2013 payment-card breach notice, written as a 'Dear Target Guest' letter that opens with brand-trust reassurance ('Our brand has been built on a 50-year foundation of trust...') before the scope of one of the largest retail breaches on record is stated. All three are dense_low_card_high: the scorecard rates this text quite high while dense rates it only moderately, suggesting dense is discounting the reassurance framing in a way the scorecard is not capturing as a distinct property.
member_names: Direct incident facts vs. reassurance-letter voice

selected.name: Independent celebrity, humor, or stunt hook
selected.instruction: Score whether the release contains a hook that would draw journalistic interest on its own, independent of any business substance: a celebrity/public-figure tie-in, deliberate humor, a stunt, or a surprising human-interest angle. A 10 = a strong, self-contained novelty/celebrity/humor hook that could carry a story by itself. A 0 = no such hook, purely conventional business content.
selected.rationale: R46 (Tesla's April Fools 'Model W' watch announcement) and R52 (Seth Rogen hosting an Airbnb stay tied to his Houseplant brand) are both dense_high_card_low: dense rates both fairly high while the scorecard rates both low, especially R52 (card_pct near the bottom of the whole slice). Neither item is 'newsworthy' in the hard-facts sense the scorecard likely rewards, but both carry an independent human-interest/novelty hook that a lifestyle or entertainment desk would plausibly cover.
member_names: Independent celebrity, humor, or stunt hook

selected.name: Operational specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the item states exactly what will change, for whom, where, when, and how it will work; score 0 when it offers only broad intentions or slogans.
selected.rationale: R12 specifies products, stores, rollout timing, and shopping mechanics, while R55 lays out concrete reopening procedures across locations.

selected.name: Strong time-sensitive news peg
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the item is anchored to a clearly dated crisis, deadline, seasonal event, live market movement, or imminent launch; score 0 when its significance is essentially timeless.
selected.rationale: R02 concerns a specific recent airport lapse, while R50 ties its analysis to rapidly changing energy prices and a defined forecast period.

selected.name: Formal wire-service dateline and ticker format
selected.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the item opens with formal newswire conventions -- a capitalized CITY, STATE/COUNTRY dateline, an explicit wire-service name (e.g., 'PRNewswire'), and/or a stock ticker in parentheses (e.g., '(NYSE: CRM)') paired with an explicit 'today announced' construction -- versus an informal blog-post or social-caption opening with no dateline, wire branding, or ticker. 0 = none of these markers present; 10 = fully formatted like a paid-financial-newswire release with dateline, wire branding, and ticker. Score only the EXTENT of this formatting; do not judge whether the formal presentation makes the underlying news more important.
selected.rationale: R26 explicitly opens 'TEANECK, N.J. and LONDON, Oct. 4, 2012 / PRNewswire /' and R40 opens 'SAN FRANCISCO -- Sept 20, 2018 -- Salesforce [NYSE: CRM] ... today announced,' both showing the full formal wire template, unlike the informal blog-style openings elsewhere in the slice (e.g., R09, R57). This is tagged mixed because SEC-regulated material announcements (mergers, offerings) are genuinely required to go out through this formal channel, so the format can coincide with real materiality as well as being a pure channel artifact.
member_names: Formal wire-service dateline and ticker format
Paid-newswire dateline, ticker and legal-trailer formalism

selected.name: Capture integrity: extraction residue and mid-sentence truncation
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text shows signs of being an incomplete or failed page capture rather than a whole self-contained document. Count: (a) stray serialisation characters with no textual role, such as a lone double-quote on its own line, a closing brace '}', or a triple-backtick fence; (b) meta-commentary that describes the page instead of being the page, e.g. sentences beginning 'The provided raw page content does not appear to contain a press release' or 'This page does not appear to contain a press release'; (c) a body that stops mid-sentence or mid-word with no closing; (d) an absent headline, dateline or opening so that the text begins abruptly in the middle of an argument; (e) collapsed whitespace runs or glued-together words where layout was lost. 0 = a clean, complete, self-contained document; 5 = the document is intact but visibly clipped at one end; 10 = the text is mostly capture residue with little or no release content in it. Score only the extent of capture damage. You must NOT judge whether the surviving content is good, and must not reward or penalise the item for what the damage hides.
selected.rationale: MODE 2. R14, R29 and R33 are the extreme case: each consists of a dangling double-quote, a '}' and a code fence, followed by a note that the page contained no press release at all - i.e. the entire item is pipeline residue. Milder truncation is widespread and equally upstream: R13 stops mid-word at 'While this educati', R01 stops at 'a ban on party ho', R23 at 'Airbnb listings were “wishli', R44 and R56 stop mid-paragraph, R52 at 'combines a passion for client s'. R31 and R47 are the same Tesla body with and without its headline line, differing only in what the capture retained. Nothing here is about the release, so not mixed.
member_names: Capture integrity: extraction residue and mid-sentence truncation

selected.name: Forwarded or republished internal communication markers
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text frames itself as a forwarded, re-posted or re-published message originally directed at an internal audience (employees, customers, community members) rather than at journalists — look for framing phrases like 'the following email was sent to,' 'below is an email,' 'the message below was posted,' or similar introductory wrapper language around what is clearly an internal memo or customer letter. Do NOT judge whether republishing was appropriate; score only how much of this framing is present.
selected.rationale: R07/R22/R26 embed a customer letter with wrapper text ('The message below was posted from Target on Dec. 19, 2013'); R12/R50 open with 'The following email was just sent to Tesla employees'; R14 introduces 'Below is an email…sent to Airbnb hosts.' This wrapping is a distribution fingerprint, not a quality signal, yet it could strongly affect how a model scores the item.
member_names: Forwarded or republished internal communication markers
Frames item as a reprinted communication

selected.name: Calendar and embargo markers
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text exposes calendar or news-cycle conventions such as quarter-end references, holiday timing, conference schedules, exact event deadlines, embargo-style dates, or “for immediate release” wording; do not judge whether the timing is good or newsworthy.
selected.rationale: R15 refers to the final weeks of a quarter, R18 provides detailed meeting deadlines, and R48 is explicitly timed around Christmas shopping. These markers can affect reception and text style independently of the event's substance.

selected.name: Character-encoding corruption (mojibake) density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH visible character-encoding corruption is present in the text. Count occurrences of: (a) apostrophes, em-dashes or curly quotes mis-rendered as a stray letter 'a' glued inside or between words, e.g. 'Itas', 'thatas', 'worldas', 'Salesforceas', 'Iam', 'Weave' (for 'we have'), 'salariesafor', 'basisamaking', 'community a our Ohana'; (b) runs of isolated capital 'A' characters standing where non-breaking spaces or bullets were, e.g. 'A A A A A'; (c) replacement boxes, question marks or stray '?' where punctuation should be, e.g. a trailing '?' in a headline; (d) sentences that break off at a dropped character, e.g. 'reach out to us at  ' with nothing following. Score 0 if the text is clean throughout; 3 if there are a handful of instances; 7 if corruption appears in most paragraphs; 10 if it is pervasive and affects reading on nearly every line. Score only how much corruption is visible. You must NOT judge whether the writing is good, and must NOT treat corruption as evidence about the care, competence or importance of the item.
selected.rationale: MODE 2. The corruption is deterministic given the source platform and the scrape, and is invisible in the document as its authors wrote it. R08 is saturated ('Itas a challenge', 'thatas just what', 'Weave completed', 'salariesafor both men and women'); R18 likewise ('the worldas #1 CRM provider', 'Salesforceas commitment', 'Iam proud to share'); R44 combines both forms ('Iam helping develop Salesforceas plan') with long 'A A A A' runs; R60 has 'our community a our Ohana' and 'forthright a which is exactly'; R13 carries a stray '?' in its headline. R41, R57, R59 and R48 are clean. Because the parent is a decoding step and nothing else, this is a pure nuisance.
selected.upstream_parent: the character encoding of the source page and the decoding step of the harvesting pipeline - which in practice tags which organisation's CMS the item was pulled from
upstream_parent_all_members: data extraction / scraping pipeline quality

selected.name: Presupposes an earlier installment in series
selected.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the text uses language that presupposes the reader already knows about a prior, un-recapped announcement in an ongoing series on this topic -- e.g., 'update on,' 'is not a new X, but was uncovered as part of the ongoing...,' 'despite extensions on previous deadlines' -- versus language that introduces the organization and topic from scratch as if for a first-time reader. 0 = fully self-contained, introduces everything from scratch; 10 = the text heavily assumes reader knowledge of an earlier, un-recapped announcement. Score only the EXTENT of this presupposition; do not judge whether the update itself is significant.
selected.rationale: R17 ('Target Provides Update on Data Breach... This theft is not a new breach, but was uncovered as part of the ongoing investigation') and R12 ('unable to reach a settlement... despite extensions on previous deadlines to negotiate a settlement') both assume the reader already tracks an earlier chapter of the story. Later installments of a fast-moving story can also be genuinely more newsworthy, so this is tagged mixed.
member_names: Presupposes an earlier installment in series

selected.name: Reactive rebuttal framing that names an external antagonist
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text is organised as a response to a specific outside actor or outside account, as opposed to a self-initiated announcement. Count: (a) a named external party - a regulator, agency, publication, television programme, petition, blog post, short-seller, court or news outlet - identified in the text; (b) that party's claims restated in order to be contradicted; (c) an enumerated refutation structure ('First ... Second ... Third ... Fourth ...') or a run of paragraphs each opening by correcting a stated allegation; (d) explicit characterisations of the outside account as false, incorrect, misleading, preposterous or spun. 0 = no outside actor is answered anywhere; 5 = an outside actor is named and briefly answered inside a longer item; 10 = the entire item exists to rebut a named outside account point by point. Score only the extent of the rebuttal structure. You must NOT judge who is right, whether the rebuttal is convincing, or whether responding was a good idea.
selected.rationale: MODE 2. Whether a release was forced by an outside event is an unseen production fact, but it leaves an unmistakable textual fingerprint. R15 names the California DFEH and answers its intended lawsuit ('A narrative spun by the DFEH and a handful of plaintiff firms'); R16 is titled 'Misfortune' and rebuts a named magazine paragraph by paragraph ('Fortune's article is fundamentally incorrect'); R21 uses the explicit 'First ... Second ... Third ... Fourth' ladder against a blog post and NHTSA reporting; R26 opens 'This petition is completely false and was brought by a Tesla short-seller'; R48 sues and answers a named BBC programme; R51 narrates an incident involving named 'RGJ' employees. R37, R39 and R42 have none of this. Tagged mixed because a genuine external controversy is often independently newsworthy, so the parent can drive real news value as well as this fingerprint.
member_names: Defensive rebuttal aimed at a named critic
Reactive rebuttal framing that names an external antagonist

selected.name: Recurring data-bulletin format
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the item follows a routine statistical bulletin format: fixed-period benchmark reporting, month-over-month or year-over-year comparisons, named indices, ranked geographies, source links, and subscription prompts; score extent only, not the importance or quality of the data.
selected.rationale: A standardized analyst-bulletin format can be highly machine-recognizable and routinely distributed without its formatting being evidence of independent news value. The nearly identical Case-Shiller structures in R22, R30, and R58 provide clear fingerprints.
selected.upstream_parent: recurring distribution or editorial desk practice

selected.name: Quantitative Data & Index Dump
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text consists primarily of dense numerical data, percentages, specific financial metrics, and index values with minimal narrative context. Do not judge the accuracy or importance of the data, only the density of the quantitative dump.
selected.rationale: R34, R36, R44, and R47 are heavy data dumps. The upstream factor is SEC or industry reporting requirements. Dense numerical text can skew scorecard evaluations for 'comprehensiveness' while dense models might perceive it as boilerplate, neither of which strictly maps to newsworthiness.
upstream_parent_all_members: compliance and reporting requirements

selected.name: Consumer Marketing Call-to-Action
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text reads like a retail advertisement or product launch aimed at consumers, featuring pricing instructions, shopping deadlines, event booking links, or promotional slogans. Do not judge the quality of the marketing, only the presence of consumer calls-to-action.
selected.rationale: R23, R33, R37, and R49 feature product placements and retail promotions (e.g., Hatchimal hunts, Target Deal Days). This upstream factor—drafting by a product marketing team rather than corporate communications—leaves clear textual calls-to-action that scorecards might misinterpret as substantive detail.
upstream_parent_all_members: product marketing practice
